blocks.md: Matrix calculus is ordinary differentiation done for many variables at once and written compactly. When a function depends on a whole vector of coefficients, its derivative is a vector of slopes, one per coefficient. Two rules — one for linear expressions, one for quadratic ones — mirror the familiar rules for ax and ax squared, and are enough to derive the least-squares formula in a few lines.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Every estimator in econometrics is derived by setting a vector derivative to zero, so these rules are the price of admission for reading derivations.

The derivative of a **scalar** $f(\mathbf{x})$ with respect to a $K\times1$ vector $\mathbf{x}$ is the $K\times1$ gradient — one partial derivative per element. Three rules cover almost all of econometrics.

| Function (scalar) | Derivative w.r.t. $\mathbf{x}$ | Scalar analogue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{x}$ (or $\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{a}$) | $\mathbf{a}$ | $ax \to a$ |
| $\mathbf{x}'A\mathbf{x}$ | $(A + A')\mathbf{x}$ | $ax^2 \to 2ax$ |
| $\mathbf{x}'A\mathbf{x}$, $A$ symmetric | $2A\mathbf{x}$ | |

sections.heading: Proof sketch of the quadratic rule

blocks.md: $\mathbf{x}'A\mathbf{x} = \sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}x_ix_j$. Differentiating with respect to $x_k$ picks up every term containing $x_k$: $\sum_j a_{kj}x_j + \sum_i a_{ik}x_i$, which is the $k$-th element of $A\mathbf{x} + A'\mathbf{x}$.
**Numerical check**: $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{x} = (1,2)'$: the rule gives $(A + A')\mathbf{x} = (6, 14)'$, and finite differences agree.

- $\mathbf{y}'\mathbf{y}$ has no $\mathbf{b}$: derivative $\mathbf{0}$.
- $-2\mathbf{b}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y})$ is linear, $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}$: derivative $-2\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}$.
- $\mathbf{b}'(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})\mathbf{b}$ is quadratic with symmetric $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$: derivative $2\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b}$.
Setting the sum to zero gives $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y}$. The Hessian $2\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$ is PD under full rank, so it is a minimum.

- Using $2A\mathbf{x}$ when $A$ is not symmetric.
- Layout conventions: some texts write gradients as rows. Pick column ("denominator") layout and check dimensions.
- Writing $\partial(\mathbf{b}'\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{y})/\partial\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{y}'\mathbf{X}$ — that is the transpose of the right answer.

- **Econometrics**: [OLS in Matrix Form](note:ols-in-matrix-form); GLS and MLE first-order conditions.
- **Optimization**: vector first-order conditions in [Unconstrained Optimization](note:unconstrained-optimization).
